text: What happens when computers start using human brains?
This is a biocomputer. And you see, those are real human neurons. Alive. On a chip.
Where from? Stem cells, grown into neurons on the chip.
Under them, a grid of fifty nine electrodes.
The silicon talks to them. Pulses in. Spikes out.
But neurons need a body. So the box becomes one.
Pumps feed them. Filters pull out waste. Gas mixing lets them breathe. Heat keeps body temperature.
They live up to six months.
But can they learn? In twenty twenty two, about eight hundred thousand neurons in a dish learned Pong.
Hit the ball? Predictable feedback. Miss? Random noise. They learned to rally.
That was DishBrain. Its successor, the CL one, sells for thirty five thousand dollars.
Or rent one. Swiss startup FinalSpark streams sixteen living mini brains online.
Why bother? Power. Your brain runs on about twenty watts. AI data centers draw hundreds of megawatts.
FinalSpark claims a million times less energy. Not proven yet.
Of course, it can't think like you. Yet. But for the first time, a computer is grown, not built.
What should we take apart next?
